subthemes.text:
OVERVIEW

[1] The appeal is dismissed. XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of China. He alleges to fear persecution from China because of his religious conversion to Christianity and his involvement in a house church. The Appellant alleges that while in China, he was detained by the Public Security Bureau (PSB) because of his involvement in the house church.

[2] The Appellant left China on XXXX XXXX, 2020, on a fraudulent passport provided by his smuggler. The Appellant made his refugee claim during his interview at the port of entry, on XXXX XXXX, 2020.

[3] The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) heard the claim on January 19, 2022. The RPD rejected the claim in its orally dictated decision on February 2, 2022, finding that the Appellant was not credible in his testimony.

[4] The Appellant appeals this decision to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD). The Appellant submits that the RPD's credibility findings cannot be upheld. The RAD carefully considered the merits of the appeal in its decision below.
DECISION

[5] The RAD dismisses the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention1 refugee nor a person in need of protection.

subthemes.text:
ANALYSIS

[8] The RPD found that the Appellant did not credibly establish his motivation for his departure from China or his desire to come to Canada.4 On three separate occasions at the Point of Entry (POE), the Appellant told border services that he desired employment and had difficulty finding work in China.5 The RPD found that this undermines his credibility and motivation for making a refugee claim, as he had the benefit of an interpreter at the hearing. At the hearing, the Appellant said that the only reason he left China was to flee religious persecution.6 The RPD considered the Appellant's state of mind at the border during the POE interview. However, the RPD found that the Appellant had the opportunity to clarify his responses at the hearing and failed to do so.7

[9] The Appellant submits that the RPD was microscopic in its finding.8 The POE asked very few questions regarding his motivation for coming to Canada.9 He was not asked to elaborate details.10 The Appellant further submits that POE interviews are conducted with specific instructions to be brief.11

[10] The RAD disagrees with the Appellant. The Appellant's motivation for coming to Canada is central to his refugee claim. The Appellant arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2020.12 Approximately nine months later, the Appellant had his interview with the border officer took place on XXXX XXXX, 2020.13 Hence, this is not a situation where the Appellant had just arrived after a long journey from China where he may have felt disoriented or stressed during the interview. Rather, the Appellant had already been living in Canada for nine months at the time of this POE interview, and regularly attending a Canadian church since XXXX XXXX, 2020.14 The RAD finds that the Appellant had time to consider how and when to make a refugee claim when he had his POE interview. Since then, the Appellant had the opportunity to experience religious freedom in Canada at the time he made his claim, and it is unclear why the Appellant could not articulate this as the main reason why he could not return to China.

[11] When the POE officer asked the Appellant why he could not return to China and what would happen to him if he returned, the Appellant made no mention of religious persecution.15 Rather, the Appellant simply indicated that it was "difficult to make a living in China."16 The RAD finds that employment opportunities are entirely different from fearing religious persecution. This inconsistency is not a matter of vagueness or brevity in the Appellant's response. Therefore, the RAD finds that the RPD's negative credibility finding is correct.

subthemes.text:
[12] The RPD found that the Appellant gave inconsistent testimony regarding the circumstances of his arrest by the PSB.17 The Appellant could not establish whether he was detained by the PSB while praying or while cleaning.18 These are two different actions. The Appellant's Canadian pastor provided a support letter indicating that the Appellant was detained by PSB in China while distributing leaflets.19 The RPD found the inconsistent explanation of the Appellant's arrest to make the letter unreliable evidence.20 The RPD further found that the date of arrest on the PSB receipt is XXXX XXXX, 2019. However, in the Appellant's Schedule 12 form, he listed his detention as XXXX XXXX, 2019.21 At the hearing, the Appellant testified that his bail money was posted on XXXX XXXX, 2019, and as result, he was released and issued the receipt. When this inconsistency was put to the Appellant, he indicated that there must have been a translation error.22 The RPD found that the Appellant did not provide a reasonable explanation and found the document not to be authentic.23

[13] The Appellant submits that the RPD's flawed findings regarding the POE inconsistencies contributed to the RPD's conclusion that the receipt could not be trusted.24 Therefore, this finding regarding the inauthentic receipt cannot be sustained.

[14] The RAD disagrees with the Appellant. The RAD finds that the receipt is unreliable evidence, and on a balance of probabilities, it is inauthentic. The original PSB receipt indicates the monetary fine was paid on the date of release as "XXXX XXXX, 2019."25 However, the Appellant testified that he was arrested on XXXX XXXX, 2019 and held overnight.26 His relatives gathered money and gave it to the PSB station to secure his release the following day.27 He was released thereafter. No explanation was given for why the payment receipt would be dated and stamped prior to payment being received the following day. The RAD finds this inconsistency to be significant to the claim, since the payment had to be made in order to secure his release. The RAD has reviewed contents of the PSB receipt showing the payment in made in full, along with the administrative punishment decision authorizing the demand for payment.28 There are no security features on either of these documents, making them easy to fabricate. Considering all these factors collectively, the RAD finds that the RPD was correct to find the receipt inauthentic.

[15] The Appellant does not challenge the RPD's findings regarding the inconsistent explanations regarding his arrest. After its independent analysis, The RAD agrees that cleaning and praying are two entirely different activities, and the Appellant did not provide a satisfactory for giving these two descriptions in his oral testimony. Also, it is uncertain how the Appellant's pastor would mistakenly indicate that the Appellant was arrested in China after distributing religious leaflets. This is a specific activity which is distinct from cleaning or praying. The RAD accepts that the Appellant regularly attended this church after arriving in Canada. However, after reviewing the contents of the letter, the RAD does not find it to be reliable evidence for the Appellant's sincerity of his beliefs or his activities in China.

[16] The RAD considers that the Appellant provided inconsistent explanations for the circumstances of his arrest and also provided an inauthentic PSB document. The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant was not arrested by PSB for any participation in religious services, and he was not held for bail.
Religious knowledge

[17] The RPD found that the Appellant had some religious knowledge of Christianity. However, the RPD found that the Appellant was unable to answer some basic questions about Christianity, despite being a religious follower for four years and having taken part in Bible studies.29 The RPD found that the Appellant incorrectly responded about the betrayal of Jesus and confused the Christian holidays of Christmas, Good Friday and Easter Sunday.30

[18] The Appellant submits that the RPD failed to consider that there is a low bar for religious knowledge.31 The Appellant submits that the RPD did not consider the sincerity of his beliefs.32 In its decision, the RPD acknowledged that the Appellant had some religious knowledge. The RPD erred by weighing the Appellant's testimony about his faith against the misguided idea of what a person in his circumstance would know or understand.33 The Appellant submits that he had limited exposure to Christina at the time he was interviewed at the POE, given that he was a member of an underground church in China.34 Therefore, he may not have possessed as much knowledge as he would have, had he been a Christian in a country where he could practice freely.35

[19] The RAD disagrees with the Appellant. While the RAD acknowledges that there is a low bar for proving religious knowledge, the RAD considers that already existing credibility concerns discussed above. Also, the RAD considers that the Appellant was asked to explain the definition of the Easter holiday at his POE interview on XXXX XXXX, 2020.36 At this point in time, he had already been attending a Christian church regularly since XXXX XXXX, 2020.37 This interview did not take place immediately after the Appellant entered Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2020, where his alleged religious experience was limited to the underground church in China. The Appellant testified that he regularly participated in Bible studies and attended religious services since coming to Canada. According to the calendar year for 2020, the Easter holiday occurred on April 12, 2020. This was nearly a month after the Appellant began regularly attending his Canadian church on XXXX XXXX, 2020. Given the centrality of the Easter celebration and the Appellant's participation in a church at the time when Easter took place, the RAD finds that the RPD was correct to impugn the Appellant's credibility on religious knowledge, and to find that any religious knowledge he may have had, was obtained to bolster his claim.
In summary

[20] The RAD finds that the Appellant is not sincere in his Christian beliefs, on a balance of probabilities. The RAD finds that the Appellant did not come to Canada with the intention of fleeing any religious persecution. The Appellant indicated that difficulty with finding employment was the main reason why he could not return to China. The RAD notes that the Appellant gave this explanation at the POE interview, nine months after he had entered Canada, and being fully aware that he was interviewed because of his intention to make a refugee claim. The Appellant also provided an inauthentic PSB payment receipt and gave inconsistent evidence regarding his arrest.

[21] The Appellant provided a baptism certificate confirming his baptism on XXXX XXXX, 2020.38 The Appellant also provided a photograph of the workplace injury which later allegedly led to his discussion of religion with his aunt in China. After its independent assessment, the RAD accepts that the Appellant participated in the baptism process at his Canadian church. The RAD also accepts that the Appellant was injured at his former workplace in China. However, the inclusion of these documents does not overcome the credibility concerns noted above.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] The appeal is dismissed. XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of China. He alleges to fear persecution from China because of his religious conversion to Christianity and his involvement in a house church. The Appellant alleges that while in China, he was detained by the Public Security Bureau (PSB) because of his involvement in the house church.
[2] The Appellant left China on XXXX XXXX, 2020, on a fraudulent passport provided by his smuggler. The Appellant made his refugee claim during his interview at the port of entry, on XXXX XXXX, 2020.

[3] The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) heard the claim on January 19, 2022. The RPD rejected the claim in its orally dictated decision on February 2, 2022, finding that the Appellant was not credible in his testimony.

[4] The Appellant appeals this decision to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD). The Appellant submits that the RPD's credibility findings cannot be upheld. The RAD carefully considered the merits of the appeal in its decision below.
DECISION
[5] The RAD dismisses the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention1 refugee nor a person in need of protection.
Standard of review

[6] The role of the RAD is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.2
No new evidence and no request for oral hearing
[7] The Appellant is not submitting any new evidence on appeal, nor is he requesting an oral hearing.3
ANALYSIS

[8] The RPD found that the Appellant did not credibly establish his motivation for his departure from China or his desire to come to Canada.4 On three separate occasions at the Point of Entry (POE), the Appellant told border services that he desired employment and had difficulty finding work in China.5 The RPD found that this undermines his credibility and motivation for making a refugee claim, as he had the benefit of an interpreter at the hearing. At the hearing, the Appellant said that the only reason he left China was to flee religious persecution.6 The RPD considered the Appellant's state of mind at the border during the POE interview. However, the RPD found that the Appellant had the opportunity to clarify his responses at the hearing and failed to do so.7

[9] The Appellant submits that the RPD was microscopic in its finding.8 The POE asked very few questions regarding his motivation for coming to Canada.9 He was not asked to elaborate details.10 The Appellant further submits that POE interviews are conducted with specific instructions to be brief.11

[10] The RAD disagrees with the Appellant. The Appellant's motivation for coming to Canada is central to his refugee claim. The Appellant arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2020.12 Approximately nine months later, the Appellant had his interview with the border officer took place on XXXX XXXX, 2020.13 Hence, this is not a situation where the Appellant had just arrived after a long journey from China where he may have felt disoriented or stressed during the interview. Rather, the Appellant had already been living in Canada for nine months at the time of this POE interview, and regularly attending a Canadian church since XXXX XXXX, 2020.14 The RAD finds that the Appellant had time to consider how and when to make a refugee claim when he had his POE interview. Since then, the Appellant had the opportunity to experience religious freedom in Canada at the time he made his claim, and it is unclear why the Appellant could not articulate this as the main reason why he could not return to China.

[11] When the POE officer asked the Appellant why he could not return to China and what would happen to him if he returned, the Appellant made no mention of religious persecution.15 Rather, the Appellant simply indicated that it was "difficult to make a living in China."16 The RAD finds that employment opportunities are entirely different from fearing religious persecution. This inconsistency is not a matter of vagueness or brevity in the Appellant's response. Therefore, the RAD finds that the RPD's negative credibility finding is correct.
PSB detention receipt and inconsistent descriptions of arrest

[12] The RPD found that the Appellant gave inconsistent testimony regarding the circumstances of his arrest by the PSB.17 The Appellant could not establish whether he was detained by the PSB while praying or while cleaning.18 These are two different actions. The Appellant's Canadian pastor provided a support letter indicating that the Appellant was detained by PSB in China while distributing leaflets.19 The RPD found the inconsistent explanation of the Appellant's arrest to make the letter unreliable evidence.20 The RPD further found that the date of arrest on the PSB receipt is XXXX XXXX, 2019. However, in the Appellant's Schedule 12 form, he listed his detention as XXXX XXXX, 2019.21 At the hearing, the Appellant testified that his bail money was posted on XXXX XXXX, 2019, and as result, he was released and issued the receipt. When this inconsistency was put to the Appellant, he indicated that there must have been a translation error.22 The RPD found that the Appellant did not provide a reasonable explanation and found the document not to be authentic.23

[13] The Appellant submits that the RPD's flawed findings regarding the POE inconsistencies contributed to the RPD's conclusion that the receipt could not be trusted.24 Therefore, this finding regarding the inauthentic receipt cannot be sustained.

[14] The RAD disagrees with the Appellant. The RAD finds that the receipt is unreliable evidence, and on a balance of probabilities, it is inauthentic. The original PSB receipt indicates the monetary fine was paid on the date of release as "XXXX XXXX, 2019."25 However, the Appellant testified that he was arrested on XXXX XXXX, 2019 and held overnight.26 His relatives gathered money and gave it to the PSB station to secure his release the following day.27 He was released thereafter. No explanation was given for why the payment receipt would be dated and stamped prior to payment being received the following day. The RAD finds this inconsistency to be significant to the claim, since the payment had to be made in order to secure his release. The RAD has reviewed contents of the PSB receipt showing the payment in made in full, along with the administrative punishment decision authorizing the demand for payment.28 There are no security features on either of these documents, making them easy to fabricate. Considering all these factors collectively, the RAD finds that the RPD was correct to find the receipt inauthentic.

[15] The Appellant does not challenge the RPD's findings regarding the inconsistent explanations regarding his arrest. After its independent analysis, The RAD agrees that cleaning and praying are two entirely different activities, and the Appellant did not provide a satisfactory for giving these two descriptions in his oral testimony. Also, it is uncertain how the Appellant's pastor would mistakenly indicate that the Appellant was arrested in China after distributing religious leaflets. This is a specific activity which is distinct from cleaning or praying. The RAD accepts that the Appellant regularly attended this church after arriving in Canada. However, after reviewing the contents of the letter, the RAD does not find it to be reliable evidence for the Appellant's sincerity of his beliefs or his activities in China.

[16] The RAD considers that the Appellant provided inconsistent explanations for the circumstances of his arrest and also provided an inauthentic PSB document. The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant was not arrested by PSB for any participation in religious services, and he was not held for bail.
Religious knowledge

[17] The RPD found that the Appellant had some religious knowledge of Christianity. However, the RPD found that the Appellant was unable to answer some basic questions about Christianity, despite being a religious follower for four years and having taken part in Bible studies.29 The RPD found that the Appellant incorrectly responded about the betrayal of Jesus and confused the Christian holidays of Christmas, Good Friday and Easter Sunday.30

[18] The Appellant submits that the RPD failed to consider that there is a low bar for religious knowledge.31 The Appellant submits that the RPD did not consider the sincerity of his beliefs.32 In its decision, the RPD acknowledged that the Appellant had some religious knowledge. The RPD erred by weighing the Appellant's testimony about his faith against the misguided idea of what a person in his circumstance would know or understand.33 The Appellant submits that he had limited exposure to Christina at the time he was interviewed at the POE, given that he was a member of an underground church in China.34 Therefore, he may not have possessed as much knowledge as he would have, had he been a Christian in a country where he could practice freely.35

[19] The RAD disagrees with the Appellant. While the RAD acknowledges that there is a low bar for proving religious knowledge, the RAD considers that already existing credibility concerns discussed above. Also, the RAD considers that the Appellant was asked to explain the definition of the Easter holiday at his POE interview on XXXX XXXX, 2020.36 At this point in time, he had already been attending a Christian church regularly since XXXX XXXX, 2020.37 This interview did not take place immediately after the Appellant entered Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2020, where his alleged religious experience was limited to the underground church in China. The Appellant testified that he regularly participated in Bible studies and attended religious services since coming to Canada. According to the calendar year for 2020, the Easter holiday occurred on April 12, 2020. This was nearly a month after the Appellant began regularly attending his Canadian church on XXXX XXXX, 2020. Given the centrality of the Easter celebration and the Appellant's participation in a church at the time when Easter took place, the RAD finds that the RPD was correct to impugn the Appellant's credibility on religious knowledge, and to find that any religious knowledge he may have had, was obtained to bolster his claim.
In summary

[20] The RAD finds that the Appellant is not sincere in his Christian beliefs, on a balance of probabilities. The RAD finds that the Appellant did not come to Canada with the intention of fleeing any religious persecution. The Appellant indicated that difficulty with finding employment was the main reason why he could not return to China. The RAD notes that the Appellant gave this explanation at the POE interview, nine months after he had entered Canada, and being fully aware that he was interviewed because of his intention to make a refugee claim. The Appellant also provided an inauthentic PSB payment receipt and gave inconsistent evidence regarding his arrest.

[21] The Appellant provided a baptism certificate confirming his baptism on XXXX XXXX, 2020.38 The Appellant also provided a photograph of the workplace injury which later allegedly led to his discussion of religion with his aunt in China. After its independent assessment, the RAD accepts that the Appellant participated in the baptism process at his Canadian church. The RAD also accepts that the Appellant was injured at his former workplace in China. However, the inclusion of these documents does not overcome the credibility concerns noted above.
[22] For the reasons provided, the RAD finds that the RPD's decision is correct and it is upheld.
CONCLUSION

[23] The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
